lead: Dedicated short-range communication (DSRC) is a short-range radio link for vehicles, centred on 5.9 GHz. IEEE 802.11p adapts Wi-Fi to moving cars: 10 MHz channels and no association handshake. WAVE, the IEEE 1609 family, adds channel timing, networking and security above it. A car broadcasts a basic safety message about ten times each second to nearby vehicles and roadside units. Only a few universities teach this stack in depth.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.6 for V2X applications and Chapter 6.7 for VANET routing.

blocks.text: DSRC uses spectrum near 5.9 GHz: about 5.85–5.925 GHz in the US and 5.855–5.925 GHz in Europe. The band is split into 10 MHz channels: one control channel (CCH) and several service channels (SCH). That width is half of ordinary 802.11a Wi-Fi, so the headline rate is about half.

IEEE 802.11p is the MAC and PHY. The PHY uses orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) and gives roughly 3 to 27 Mbit/s depending on modulation and coding. Lower rates survive longer links and more Doppler.

The MAC is Wi-Fi adapted for cars. A vehicle works outside a basic service set, so it does not associate, authenticate or exchange keys before sending. It waits for an idle channel and broadcasts. Enhanced Distributed Channel Access (EDCA) gives four access categories, so urgent safety frames wait less than ordinary data. This is connectionless broadcast, not a phone call. The radio is half-duplex: one unit cannot transmit and receive on the same channel at the same moment.
WAVE (Wireless Access in Vehicular Environments) is the IEEE 1609 set above 802.11p. It shares one radio among safety, traffic and internet traffic.

items: IEEE 1609.1 is a resource manager; an application can request services from another unit. Simple safety systems rarely use it.
IEEE 1609.2 defines security. Signed and encrypted messages with public-key certificates let a receiver check origin and integrity.
IEEE 1609.3 is networking. WSMP (WAVE Short Message Protocol) carries small safety packets with low overhead; IPv6 carries ordinary internet traffic.

IEEE 1609.4 coordinates the radio. A 100 ms sync interval splits into a control-channel interval and a service-channel interval, commonly 50 ms each. During CCH time vehicles tune to the control channel for announcements and safety; during SCH time they switch to a service channel for other data.

blocks.text: An onboard unit sends a basic safety message (BSM) about ten times per second, carrying position, speed, heading and braking. Neighbours build a local picture even without line of sight.

examples.question: A 300-byte BSM is sent at 6 Mbit/s. How long is one transmission, and how many fit in a 50 ms control-channel interval that keeps 10% for overhead?
steps: Transmission time = 2400 bits / (6×10⁶ bit/s) = 4×10⁻⁴ s = 0.4 ms.
Only whole messages fit, so 112 messages fit.
examples.answer: One BSM lasts 0.4 ms; the usable interval is 45.0 ms, so the division gives 112.5 and 112 whole messages fit.

bits = 300 * 8
rate = 6e6
t_ms = bits / rate * 1000
usable_ms = 50 * (1 - 0.10)
n = usable_ms / t_ms
whole = int(n)
print(t_ms)
print(usable_ms)
print(n)
print(whole)

traps: 802.11p uses 10 MHz channels, not the 20 MHz of 802.11a, so its headline rate is roughly half.
WAVE is not another name for 802.11p. WAVE adds the IEEE 1609 layers; 802.11p is only MAC and PHY.
The control channel is for short safety and control frames, not long downloads; bulk service traffic belongs on a service channel.
The 100 ms sync interval is a radio timing rule; it does not mean a BSM must be sent exactly every 100 ms or that only one BSM fits.
3–27 Mbit/s is the PHY rate before contention and overhead; do not use it as delivered throughput in a crowded channel.

quiz.q: What band and channel width does DSRC use?
Why can 802.11p skip association and authentication before sending?
quiz.a: Cars need immediate broadcast safety frames; outside a basic service set there is no handshake to wait for.

quiz.q: A 200-byte frame is sent at 3 Mbit/s. What is its airtime?
Why does IEEE 1609.4 alternate control-channel and service-channel intervals?
quiz.a: One radio must serve both common safety/control and longer service traffic; timed switching lets all vehicles meet on the control channel.

quiz.q: Name the four IEEE 1609 layers and one job for each.
quiz.a: 1609.1 resource manager; 1609.2 security; 1609.3 networking (WSMP, IPv6); 1609.4 multi-channel timing.

quiz.q: Why is the headline 802.11p rate about half that of 802.11a?
quiz.a: 802.11p uses 10 MHz channels; 802.11a uses 20 MHz, so the same modulation carries half the bits per second.

beyond: Not for the exam. DSRC at 5.9 GHz is being challenged by cellular V2X (C-V2X) in several markets, while IEEE 802.11bd is the planned evolution of 802.11p. Security work centres on 1609.2 certificates and revocation lists, because a signed BSM is only useful if the sender's credentials are current. Search for IEEE 802.11bd, C-V2X PC5, and ETSI ITS-G5 to compare the radio families. Read the 1609.4 channel-timing rules next if you work on radio scheduling.
